question: The serious irregularities found in the management of breast cancer screening programmes in Spain undermine the principle that health is a fundamental right. It has emerged in recent months that, in Andalusia and other regions in Spain, data on screening invitations, participation and diagnostic outcomes for the population have not been fully recorded or reported.

This raises concerns vis-a-vis Council Recommendation of 9 December 2022, which calls on Member States to ensure that at least 90 % of the eligible population receive an invitation for screening by 2025.

At the same time, Spain has acquired mammography equipment using EU funds, including La Gomera (EUR 182 413, of which EUR 155 051 came from the European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) budget for 2014-2020) and Yecla (Murcia), listed as ‘eligible’ for REACT-EU funding. What is more, under the national AMAT-I plan, Spain has bought 61 mammography machines worth in excess of EUR 15.5 million.
As no comprehensive national inventory exists, it is impossible to verify potential EU co-financing and actual screening activity. In the light of the above: 1.
Does the Commission plan to carry out a specific audit of ERDF/REACT-EU mammography equipment operations?
Does it consider it necessary to ask Spain to publish harmonised screening data on a regular basis, in an open format?
Will it clarify whether the EU-funded investments and AMAT-I purchases are in keeping with the requirement to provide a transparent and verifiable screening programme?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (28.1.2026) 1. Under Cohesion policy rules, Member States are primarily responsible for preventing, detecting, and correcting irregularities, and for having effective and proportionate management and control systems, including appropriate audit coverage of all programmes through representative samples of operations and system audits.

The Commission carries out controls and audits to obtain assurance on the functioning of Member States’ systems. Each year, the Commission services draw up a rolling two-year audit plan based on a detailed risk assessment. It considers all available information and prioritises for audit the areas presenting the highest risks. The plan will be updated mid-2026. 2.

Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/22941 requires that Member States provide the Commission with a set of reference metadata and quality reports on a defined array of health data, including on cancer screening programmes. The 2022 Council Recommendation on cancer screening2 recommends Member States to report to the Commission on the implementation of this Recommendation.

These data will be compiled in the third EU cancer screening monitoring report, which is under preparation. The performance indicators have been defined through the EU4Health-funded project CanScreen-ECIS3, including invitation coverage, participation and detection rates. 3.

According to Article 168(7) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Member States are responsible for defining their health policy and for organising and delivering health services and medical care, including organisation of breast screening programmes.
All investments supported by the EU funds must, however, comply with the applicable Regulations, notably the transparency and verifiability requirements for selected operations.
